chunk_findings.detail: `tokens_list` is an operator-only verb under the change’s stated intent, but unlike `pair`, `rotate`, and `revoke` it never passes the caller’s identity (`agent`) to any auth service and has no role check. It only calls `AU.rows(st, everything=bool(args.get("all")))`, even though `agent` is discarded after `_load`. A non-operator caller can therefore invoke `tokens_list` directly and receive all issued-token records (`name`, `role`, `state`, expiry, id, by) with no `AU.AuthRefused` refusal path.

chunk_findings.detail: `_positive` only checks that each value is a positive integer, so a configuration with `agent.token_ttl_h = 721` while `agent.token_max_ttl_h` stays at the default `720` is accepted. According to the docs on these two knobs, `token_ttl_h` is the TTL used when `ddflow pair --ttl-h` is omitted, and `token_max_ttl_h` is the longest TTL `ddflow pair --ttl-h` may ask for. With this accepted input, a normal `ddflow pair` without `--ttl-h` would use 721 hours, exceeding the configured maximum; the service must then either reject its own default pairing or mint a token beyond `token_max_ttl_h`. There is no cross-knob validation enforcing `token_ttl_h <= token_max_ttl_h`.

chunk_findings.detail: `_find` matches `who` against both a token’s id and its name without deciding which namespace wins. `_NAME` allows 12-character hex names, and token ids are exactly 12 hex, so one live token’s name can equal another live token’s id. `revoke` and `rotate` then operate on whichever row `_find` encounters first; with the sorted store key, an id match can shadow the name match. Concretely, with tokens id `deadbeef0001`/name `alice` and id `deadbeef0002`/name `deadbeef0001`, `ddflow tokens revoke deadbeef0001` revokes `alice` instead of the token named `deadbeef0001`, leaving the intended token live. `_taken` only checks names, so it does not prevent this collision when the conflicting name is created.

The document itself says “a shell that unsets them passes.” Thus on a default install, `ddflow approve`, `grant add`, or `reviewers approve` can be run by an unauthenticated local invocation with `DDFLOW_AGENT` unset, so operator-only verbs remain enforced by convention, not by role. chunk_findings.detail: The guide says `token.issued` and `token.revoked` events record “who, when, the role and the expiry,” but the `token.revoked` event kind in the fixture defines only `by`, `id`, `name`, and `reason`; there is no `role` or `expires_at` field. Any consumer or audit tool that reads a `token.revoked` event expecting the documented role or expiry will find the fields absent. Either the event schema is missing the promised fields or the documentation is wrong.

The autouse fixture `_a_person` only calls `ID.clear_credential()`, not a corresponding proof-mode reset. Running this test file in declared order makes the very next test, `test_required_mode_is_off_by_default_and_changes_nothing`, fail because `ID.agent_marker()` now returns the forced `"operator token"` marker instead of `""`. chunk_findings.detail: The test sets `AU.TOKEN_ENV` to an operator token, calls `AU.bind_env(proj, Config(), ("mcp",))`, and only asserts that the return is `None` and `ID.credential()` is `None`. It never asserts `AU.TOKEN_ENV not in os.environ`. A `bind_env` implementation that returns `None` for the mcp path without removing the token from the environment would pass both assertions, yet leave the operator token in `os.environ`; subsequent subprocesses launched from that process inherit it and become operator, which is exactly the credential leak the docstring is meant to prevent.

chunk_findings.detail: In `bind_env`, `path` is checked against `_NO_TOKEN` (`(("mcp",), ("tokens", "redeem"))`), but `path` represents tuples of command components (e.g. `("tokens", "redeem")`), whereas `path` can also be a single-element tuple or different length. If a user runs a top-level command like `ddflow mcp`, `path` is `("mcp",)`, which matches `_NO_TOKEN`. However, if the command path contains subcommands or is nested differently (e.g., `("v1", "mcp")`), it will not match `_NO_TOKEN`. More importantly, if `path` is a subcommand group or a single verb, the authorization check uses `" ".join(path)`, but `_NO_TOKEN` comparison is exact tuple matching (`path in _NO_TOKEN`), causing a command like `ddflow mcp start` (path `("mcp", "start")`) to fail to match `_NO_TOKEN`, leading to token consumption or requirement when it should be exempt.

chunk_findings.detail: The bootstrap branch does not do what its contract says, and it never closes. `if not why: return` already lets a marker-free terminal mint; the following `first and lacks_only_proof and not _live_operator` branch then also lets a marked caller (the prompt-injection case this module says it holds against) mint. It does not require `role` to be operator, and `_live_operator` only looks at stored tokens, not pairings. Input: empty store, `requested_agent` for which `agent_marker` is set and `lacks_only_proof` is true, `start_pairing(..., role="reviewer")` (or `operator`). `_person` returns, the pairing code is returned to that caller, and `redeem` will trade it for a bearer token with no identity check. Minting only non-operator roles leaves `_live_operator` false, so the same caller can repeat this indefinitely.

chunk_findings.detail: Token ids are 12 hex chars and names may be the same shape, but `_find` treats `who` as either id or name and returns the first dict hit. `start_pairing` only rejects a duplicate name, not a name equal to an existing id. Input: live token id `abc123abc123` name `laptop`, then `pair abc123abc123`. After redeem, `revoke("abc123abc123")` / `rotate` deletes whichever row is iterated first and leaves the other credential live.

chunk_findings.detail: Rotation records `token.revoked` inside `log.transaction()` before `_changing` persists the store, and `verify` trusts only the store. Input: redeem of a rotation code, log transaction commits, then `atomic_write` fails (or the process dies before `_settle`). The old token row is still on disk, so `verify` still accepts it after the log says it was rotated.

chunk_findings.detail: `tokens redeem` is on the same command table the module says `ddflow serve` dispatches, but `_redeem` drops `_args` and `_read_code` always reads the server process stdin (`getpass` if that stdin is a tty, otherwise `readline`). There is no `Param` for the code. A client that posts the pairing code in the request therefore never supplies it: a non-tty serve process redeems `""` or an unrelated stdin line and fails or burns the wrong secret, and a tty serve process blocks in `getpass` on the host terminal instead of the caller.

chunk_findings.detail: The `start_pairing` function checks `_taken(data, name)` to ensure a name does not already have a live token or waiting pairing, but it does so *outside* or *concurrently* without verifying whether `name` is validly claimed by an already-stored token that might have expired or been removed, or more critically, `_taken` iterates over all tokens/pairings while `_changing` holds the file lock, but `start_pairing` calls `_person` before checking `_taken`, yet `_person` itself is called without checking the role against `cfg.agent.roles` first, leading to a potential race condition where duplicate active tokens for the same identity can be minted if two pairing requests for the same `name` interleave between `_person` and `_taken` inside the file lock context.

chunk_findings.detail: In `_read_code`, if `sys.stdin` is not a tty and `sys.stdin.readline()` is called, it returns `""` when EOF is reached, but `sys.stdin` itself can be `None` in certain non-interactive execution environments (such as some daemon or embedded test contexts), causing `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'isatty'` because the check `sys.stdin is not None and sys.stdin.isatty()` short-circuits the type safety, but the subsequent ternary `sys.stdin.readline() if sys.stdin is not None else ""` checks `sys.stdin is not None`, yet the earlier line `sys.stdin.isatty()` will crash with `AttributeError` when `sys.stdin` is `None` because the outer conjunction evaluates `sys.stdin is not None and sys.stdin.isatty()` where `sys.stdin` is `None` (evaluated as False) EXCEPT if `sys.stdin` is NOT `None` it calls `isatty()`. Wait, if `sys.stdin` is `None`, `sys.stdin is not None` is False, so it short-circuits. chunk_findings.detail: `_positive` only checks that each value is a positive integer, so a configuration with `agent.token_ttl_h = 721` while `agent.token_max_ttl_h` stays at the default `720` is accepted. Concretely, with tokens id `deadbeef0001`/name `alice` and id `deadbeef0002`/name `deadbeef0001`, `ddflow tokens revoke deadbeef0001` revokes `alice` instead of the token named `deadbeef0001`, leaving the intended token live. `_taken` only checks names, so it does not prevent this collision when the conflicting name is created.

More importantly, if `path` is a subcommand group or a single verb, the authorization check uses `" ".join(path)`, but `_NO_TOKEN` comparison is exact tuple matching (`path in _NO_TOKEN`), causing a command like `ddflow mcp start` (path `("mcp", "start")`) to fail to match `_NO_TOKEN`, leading to token consumption or requirement when it should be exempt.

chunk_findings.detail: In `_read_code`, if `sys.stdin` is not a tty and `sys.stdin.readline()` is called, it returns `""` when EOF is reached, but `sys.stdin` itself can be `None` in certain non-interactive execution environments (such as some daemon or embedded test contexts), causing `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'isatty'` because the check `sys.stdin is not None and sys.stdin.isatty()` short-circuits the type safety, but the subsequent ternary `sys.stdin.readline() if sys.stdin is not None else ""` checks `sys.stdin is not None`, yet the earlier line `sys.stdin.isatty()` will crash with `AttributeError` when `sys.stdin` is `None` because the outer conjunction evaluates `sys.stdin is not None and sys.stdin.isatty()` where `sys.stdin` is `None` (evaluated as False) EXCEPT if `sys.stdin` is NOT `None` it calls `isatty()`. Wait, if `sys.stdin` is `None`, `sys.stdin is not None` is False, so it short-circuits. But if `sys.stdin` is closed or missing its `isatty` attribute (like a StringIO mocked in tests), calling `sys.stdin.isatty()` raises `AttributeError: 'StringIO' object has no attribute 'isatty'`.

chunk_findings.detail: `start_pairing` calls `_person(..., first=True)` only after `_changing` has already dropped every store row with `expires <= now`. `_live_operator` then looks only at what remains, so once the last operator token's TTL passes, an agent whose marker is solely a missing proof (`lacks_only_proof`) is treated as the bootstrap caller and may `ddflow pair <name> --role operator` and redeem a new operator token. The same path reopens if that token is revoked. Bootstrap was only meant so a marker-free host could mint the first credential under `require_operator_token`.

chunk_findings.detail: `_find` returns the first row whose id or name equals `who`, in insertion order. Token ids are 12 hex chars and names may be the same shape, so given token id `deadbeef0001` named `alice` and a later token named `deadbeef0001`, `revoke`/`rotate` of that name hits `alice` and leaves the named token in place.

chunk_findings.detail: The store row is deleted and the lock released before `log.append(token.revoked)`. `tokens list` is derived from the log. If that append fails (disk full, handler error), a retry cannot find a live row, so it raises and never writes `token.revoked`; the token stays listed active while `verify` rejects it.

Given `_PROOF_REQUIRED` set, no `DDFLOW_AGENT`/`--agent`, `_MCP_CALL` false, and `via_mcp=True`, `is_agent` returns a refusal string while `lacks_only_proof` returns True, so a pairing exemption keyed on `lacks_only_proof` mints an operator token on the MCP surface the refusal path already knows is not a terminal.

chunk_findings.detail: Context setup always calls `ID.clear_credential()` and only rebinds when `DDFLOW_TOKEN` is set or `require_operator_token` is on. A server that follows `with_credential` (the documented non-CLI path) and then builds this context loses the proof for the whole request: `clear_credential` sets the contextvar to None, `bind_env` is skipped, and `with_credential`'s `reset` runs only after the request. Operator role checks and `resolve` therefore see no token even though verification already succeeded.

chunk_findings.detail: `_find` now compares every live token’s `name` before checking whether `who` is a token id. `start_pairing` still allows a name that is identical to another token’s id (it only prevents duplicate names, not id/name collisions). Concretely, with live token A id `deadbeef0001` named `alice`, and a later live token B named `deadbeef0001`, `revoke`/`rotate deadbeef0001` now returns token B. If the caller intended to revoke/rotate token A by its id, the wrong token is acted on and token A remains live and unreachable by id while token B exists. Preventing a name from colliding with any live token id, or requiring an explicit `id:`/`name:` disambiguator, would avoid silently targeting the wrong token.

chunk_findings.detail: The new ordering commits the token-store mutation before the audit-log transaction. `_changing` inserts the new token and, for a rotation, pops the old token; the lock is then released. Only afterwards does `log.transaction()` append `token.issued`/`token.revoked`. If that log append raises (for example the log filesystem is full), `redeem` raises so the caller never receives the new secret, but the store is already committed: the old rotated token is dead, the pairing code has been spent by `_spend`, and the new live token row keeps the client name taken until its TTL. Even without a failure, another process running `tokens list` in the gap between `_changing` and `log.transaction()` sees the old token still listed as active while `verify` already rejects it because the store row is gone. This is the same effect-before-record inconsistency as the previously accepted revoke issue, now newly introduced into `redeem`.

chunk_findings.detail: A non-rotation redeem now commits the store (code spent, token hash written) before `log.append`, and any exception there skips `return Minted`. Previously that append sat inside `_changing`, whose non-`AuthRefused` path wrote nothing, so a failed issue did not burn the code. Given a fresh pairing code and `log.append` raising (disk full, handler error), the client never receives `ddft_…`, a retry is refused because the code is gone, and the name stays taken by a hash of a secret that exists only in the failed stack frame. The rotation case is the tradeoff the new docstring describes; the first-issue path has no old token to protect and only regresses the guarantee the removed `_changing` comment stated.

chunk_findings.detail: Removing `ID.clear_credential()` leaves a proof installed by an earlier `bind_env` in the same context. data.body:
ddflow pair (one-time code shown to the operator at the host) mints a token for a named client with a role; stored hashed under the user-level dir, never in the project; ttl, rotation, revoke; ddflow tokens list|revoke; a token's name sets the agent identity (as_agent cannot override it); events token.issued/revoked in the log without secrets. Roles, ttl and per-role verb lists are config (D-everything-configurable).

Scope of the role check (amended 2026-11-05, operator, D-operator-token-default): a presented token is held to its role on every call, and every operator-only verb asks that one check. This does NOT close the gap by default: with no token presented, operator-only verbs still go by agent markers, so a shell that unsets them passes as the operator, as today. [agent].require_operator_token closes it and ships off (r-safe-by-default); shell access to the machine is the trust boundary. With no live operator token, a marker-free shell may mint one, so expiry can be recovered. Do not claim the gap is closed.
data.title: Real authentication: pairing-minted bearer tokens with roles, hashed on disk, expiring, revocable; a presented token is held to its role, the no-token gap stays open by default

data.body: D-operator-token-default keeps [agent].require_operator_token off, so with no token a marker-free shell passes as the operator. Once pairing needs no host terminal (DX-tokens-chat-route), ask the operator whether to change the default, with an upgrade path for existing projects: a knob_changed fragment, a notice, and a first-token flow that cannot lock anyone out. Enforcement by default needs the operator's choice (r-safe-by-default).

chunk_findings.detail: `tokens_list` is an operator-only verb under the change’s stated intent, but unlike `pair`, `rotate`, and `revoke` it never passes the caller’s identity (`agent`) to any auth service and has no role check. It only calls `AU.rows(st, everything=bool(args.get("all")))`, even though `agent` is discarded after `_load`. A non-operator caller can therefore invoke `tokens_list` directly and receive all issued-token records (`name`, `role`, `state`, expiry, id, by) with no `AU.AuthRefused` refusal path.

chunk_findings.detail: `_positive` only checks that each value is a positive integer, so a configuration with `agent.token_ttl_h = 721` while `agent.token_max_ttl_h` stays at the default `720` is accepted. According to the docs on these two knobs, `token_ttl_h` is the TTL used when `ddflow pair --ttl-h` is omitted, and `token_max_ttl_h` is the longest TTL `ddflow pair --ttl-h` may ask for. With this accepted input, a normal `ddflow pair` without `--ttl-h` would use 721 hours, exceeding the configured maximum; the service must then either reject its own default pairing or mint a token beyond `token_max_ttl_h`. There is no cross-knob validation enforcing `token_ttl_h <= token_max_ttl_h`.

chunk_findings.detail: `_find` matches `who` against both a token’s id and its name without deciding which namespace wins. `_NAME` allows 12-character hex names, and token ids are exactly 12 hex, so one live token’s name can equal another live token’s id. `revoke` and `rotate` then operate on whichever row `_find` encounters first; with the sorted store key, an id match can shadow the name match. Concretely, with tokens id `deadbeef0001`/name `alice` and id `deadbeef0002`/name `deadbeef0001`, `ddflow tokens revoke deadbeef0001` revokes `alice` instead of the token named `deadbeef0001`, leaving the intended token live. `_taken` only checks names, so it does not prevent this collision when the conflicting name is created.

chunk_findings.detail: The test sets `AU.TOKEN_ENV` to an operator token, calls `AU.bind_env(proj, Config(), ("mcp",))`, and only asserts that the return is `None` and `ID.credential()` is `None`. It never asserts `AU.TOKEN_ENV not in os.environ`. A `bind_env` implementation that returns `None` for the mcp path without removing the token from the environment would pass both assertions, yet leave the operator token in `os.environ`; subsequent subprocesses launched from that process inherit it and become operator, which is exactly the credential leak the docstring is meant to prevent.

chunk_findings.detail: In `bind_env`, `path` is checked against `_NO_TOKEN` (`(("mcp",), ("tokens", "redeem"))`), but `path` represents tuples of command components (e.g. `("tokens", "redeem")`), whereas `path` can also be a single-element tuple or different length. If a user runs a top-level command like `ddflow mcp`, `path` is `("mcp",)`, which matches `_NO_TOKEN`. However, if the command path contains subcommands or is nested differently (e.g., `("v1", "mcp")`), it will not match `_NO_TOKEN`. More importantly, if `path` is a subcommand group or a single verb, the authorization check uses `" ".join(path)`, but `_NO_TOKEN` comparison is exact tuple matching (`path in _NO_TOKEN`), causing a command like `ddflow mcp start` (path `("mcp", "start")`) to fail to match `_NO_TOKEN`, leading to token consumption or requirement when it should be exempt.

chunk_findings.detail: By moving `with log.transaction()` after `_changing` exits, the store is durably updated before the `token.issued`/`token.revoked` events exist. chunk_findings.detail: The new `_find` collapses the previous name-first/id-second lookup into `if who in (token_id, row["name"])`, while `start_pairing` now rejects newly paired names whose shape could be a token id. That invariant is enforced only when pairing a new name; existing persisted stores written under the prior code (`STORE_VERSION` is unchanged) can still contain a token named exactly another live token's 12-hex id. For such a store, `_find("deadbeef0001")` returns whichever of the colliding token-id row and the name-match row happens to be iterated first in `data["tokens"].items()`. Concretely, with row `deadbeef0001`/name `alice` and row `deadbeef0002`/name `deadbeef0001`, the old code always matched the name `deadbeef0001` and returned `deadbeef0002`; the new code returns `deadbeef0001` if that row is first in the dict, so `tokens revoke deadbeef0001` can revoke a different credential than before and leave the intended live token intact. The new `start_pairing` check does not address rows already on disk, so upgrading does not clear the ambiguity.

Wait, if `sys.stdin` is `None`, `sys.stdin is not None` is False, so it short-circuits. chunk_findings.detail: `_find` now compares every live token’s `name` before checking whether `who` is a token id. `start_pairing` still allows a name that is identical to another token’s id (it only prevents duplicate names, not id/name collisions). chunk_findings.detail: The new ordering commits the token-store mutation before the audit-log transaction. `_changing` inserts the new token and, for a rotation, pops the old token; the lock is then released. Only afterwards does `log.transaction()` append `token.issued`/`token.revoked`. If that log append raises (for example the log filesystem is full), `redeem` raises so the caller never receives the new secret, but the store is already committed: the old rotated token is dead, the pairing code has been spent by `_spend`, and the new live token row keeps the client name taken until its TTL. Even without a failure, another process running `tokens list` in the gap between `_changing` and `log.transaction()` sees the old token still listed as active while `verify` already rejects it because the store row is gone. This is the same effect-before-record inconsistency as the previously accepted revoke issue, now newly introduced into `redeem`.

chunk_findings.detail: A non-rotation redeem now commits the store (code spent, token hash written) before `log.append`, and any exception there skips `return Minted`. Given a fresh pairing code and `log.append` raising (disk full, handler error), the client never receives `ddft_…`, a retry is refused because the code is gone, and the name stays taken by a hash of a secret that exists only in the failed stack frame. The rotation case is the tradeoff the new docstring describes; the first-issue path has no old token to protect and only regresses the guarantee the removed `_changing` comment stated.

A transient audit-log write error can therefore lock the rotating client out while leaving the security state changed and undocumented; the store write and event-log write are not atomic.

chunk_findings.detail: The operator-only boundary is still convention, not role. That is the gap this change’s intent says the role check closes; these edits only restate the exception (`pair` after the last operator token expires) and do not turn the check on. chunk_findings.detail: The new `_find` collapses the previous name-first/id-second lookup into `if who in (token_id, row["name"])`, while `start_pairing` now rejects newly paired names whose shape could be a token id. That invariant is enforced only when pairing a new name; existing persisted stores written under the prior code (`STORE_VERSION` is unchanged) can still contain a token named exactly another live token's 12-hex id. For such a store, `_find("deadbeef0001")` returns whichever of the colliding token-id row and the name-match row happens to be iterated first in `data["tokens"].items()`. Concretely, with row `deadbeef0001`/name `alice` and row `deadbeef0002`/name `deadbeef0001`, the old code always matched the name `deadbeef0001` and returned `deadbeef0002`; the new code returns `deadbeef0001` if that row is first in the dict, so `tokens revoke deadbeef0001` can revoke a different credential than before and leave the intended live token intact. The new `start_pairing` check does not address rows already on disk, so upgrading does not clear the ambiguity.

chunk_findings.detail: The `effect` string says `on, a shell with no token is refused those verbs`, where “those verbs” refers to the operator-only verbs named in `why`. The upgrade note therefore misdescribes the behavior an operator gets when they turn the knob on: it says every operator-only verb is refused without a token, while the bootstrap `pair` is deliberately not. chunk_findings.detail: `_find` now compares every live token’s `name` before checking whether `who` is a token id. `start_pairing` still allows a name that is identical to another token’s id (it only prevents duplicate names, not id/name collisions). Concretely, with live token A id `deadbeef0001` named `alice`, and a later live token B named `deadbeef0001`, `revoke`/`rotate deadbeef0001` now returns token B. chunk_findings.detail: The new ordering commits the token-store mutation before the audit-log transaction. `_changing` inserts the new token and, for a rotation, pops the old token; the lock is then released. Only afterwards does `log.transaction()` append `token.issued`/`token.revoked`. If that log append raises (for example the log filesystem is full), `redeem` raises so the caller never receives the new secret, but the store is already committed: the old rotated token is dead, the pairing code has been spent by `_spend`, and the new live token row keeps the client name taken until its TTL. Even without a failure, another process running `tokens list` in the gap between `_changing` and `log.transaction()` sees the old token still listed as active while `verify` already rejects it because the store row is gone. This is the same effect-before-record inconsistency as the previously accepted revoke issue, now newly introduced into `redeem`.

More importantly, if `path` is a subcommand group or a single verb, the authorization check uses `" ".join(path)`, but `_NO_TOKEN` comparison is exact tuple matching (`path in _NO_TOKEN`), causing a command like `ddflow mcp start` (path `("mcp", "start")`) to fail to match `_NO_TOKEN`, leading to token consumption or requirement when it should be exempt.

chunk_findings.detail: The bootstrap branch does not do what its contract says, and it never closes. `if not why: return` already lets a marker-free terminal mint; the following `first and lacks_only_proof and not _live_operator` branch then also lets a marked caller (the prompt-injection case this module says it holds against) mint. It does not require `role` to be operator, and `_live_operator` only looks at stored tokens, not pairings. Input: empty store, `requested_agent` for which `agent_marker` is set and `lacks_only_proof` is true, `start_pairing(..., role="reviewer")` (or `operator`). `_person` returns, the pairing code is returned to that caller, and `redeem` will trade it for a bearer token with no identity check. Minting only non-operator roles leaves `_live_operator` false, so the same caller can repeat this indefinitely.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/auth.py:_person

chunk_findings.detail: Token ids are 12 hex chars and names may be the same shape, but `_find` treats `who` as either id or name and returns the first dict hit. `start_pairing` only rejects a duplicate name, not a name equal to an existing id. Input: live token id `abc123abc123` name `laptop`, then `pair abc123abc123`. After redeem, `revoke("abc123abc123")` / `rotate` deletes whichever row is iterated first and leaves the other credential live.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/auth.py:_find

chunk_findings.detail: Rotation records `token.revoked` inside `log.transaction()` before `_changing` persists the store, and `verify` trusts only the store. Input: redeem of a rotation code, log transaction commits, then `atomic_write` fails (or the process dies before `_settle`). The old token row is still on disk, so `verify` still accepts it after the log says it was rotated.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/auth.py:redeem

chunk_findings.detail: `tokens redeem` is on the same command table the module says `ddflow serve` dispatches, but `_redeem` drops `_args` and `_read_code` always reads the server process stdin (`getpass` if that stdin is a tty, otherwise `readline`). There is no `Param` for the code. A client that posts the pairing code in the request therefore never supplies it: a non-tty serve process redeems `""` or an unrelated stdin line and fails or burns the wrong secret, and a tty serve process blocks in `getpass` on the host terminal instead of the caller.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/declared/serve.py:37

chunk_findings.detail: `require_operator_token` is still `knob(False, ...)`; this diff only edits its doc string. On a default install the operator-only boundary remains the absence of an agent marker, so a shell with `DDFLOW_AGENT`/`DDFLOW_TOKEN` unset can still run operator-only verbs such as `approve`. That is exactly the convention-gated gap the intent says this change closes. The author’s triage says this is “kept”, so the previous confirmed finding still holds.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/config_sections/agent.py:require_operator_token

chunk_findings.detail: By moving `with log.transaction()` after `_changing` exits, the store is durably updated before the `token.issued`/`token.revoked` events exist. The two resources are still not committed atomically. If the process dies after `_changing` commits but before/during the log transaction, `redeem` never reaches `return Minted`, yet the one-time code has already been spent and the old token row has been popped or the new row inserted. A retry with the same code fails, so the legitimate holder ends up with no credential and no audit record. This is the reverse partial-failure mode of the old defect; the added rotation test only proves the old token is dead, not that the operation is atomic or the caller can recover.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/auth.py:redeem

chunk_findings.detail: The new text still states that `require_operator_token` is off by default and that a marker-free shell passes operator-only verbs. On a default install, `DDFLOW_AGENT` unset and no token, a local invocation of an operator-only verb such as `ddflow approve` is accepted, so the change still leaves the operator boundary enforced by convention rather than role. This is previous finding 7; the rewritten `ddflow pair` sentence does not alter the unauthenticated default path.
chunk_findings.location: docs/guide/tokens.md near “This is off by default”
chunk_findings.title: docs/guide/tokens.md near “This is off by default”

chunk_findings.detail: The new test shows the prior `_find`/`start_pairing` namespace defect is not actually fixed: it creates a live token whose name is another live token’s 12-hex id (`alias = first.split("_")[1]`), so `start_pairing` still lets a token name collide with an existing live token id. Then `tokens revoke alias` revokes the name-match token and leaves the token whose id is `alias` alive. Since `revoke`/`rotate` accept either name or id, an operator passing a live token’s id as the handle now deletes a different credential and leaves the intended one active. Making `_find` prefer names does not eliminate the collision; it only flips which identifier is shadowed.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_auth_tokens.py:test_a_name_that_reads_like_a_token_id_reaches_its_own_token

chunk_findings.detail: This test pins a partially-applied state change: with `log.append` forced to raise `OSError`, `AU.redeem` both raises and still invalidates the old token in the store. For a `tokens rotate` caller this means the command returns failure and never returns the newly minted token, yet the old token no longer verifies and no `token.issued`/`token.revoked` event is recorded, contrary to the intent’s event guarantee. A transient audit-log write error can therefore lock the rotating client out while leaving the security state changed and undocumented; the store write and event-log write are not atomic.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_auth_tokens.py:test_a_rotation_that_cannot_be_recorded_still_ends_the_old_token

chunk_findings.detail: The operator-only boundary is still convention, not role. The guide still says that with the default `require_operator_token` left false, a shell with no token passes `approve` / `grant add` / `reviewers approve` simply by not carrying an agent marker, and that enforcement is opt-in. That is the gap this change’s intent says the role check closes; these edits only restate the exception (`pair` after the last operator token expires) and do not turn the check on. A default install therefore still accepts an unauthenticated local `ddflow approve` with `DDFLOW_AGENT` unset.
chunk_findings.title: docs/guide/tokens.md:54

chunk_findings.detail: The new `_find` collapses the previous name-first/id-second lookup into `if who in (token_id, row["name"])`, while `start_pairing` now rejects newly paired names whose shape could be a token id. That invariant is enforced only when pairing a new name; existing persisted stores written under the prior code (`STORE_VERSION` is unchanged) can still contain a token named exactly another live token's 12-hex id. For such a store, `_find("deadbeef0001")` returns whichever of the colliding token-id row and the name-match row happens to be iterated first in `data["tokens"].items()`. Concretely, with row `deadbeef0001`/name `alice` and row `deadbeef0002`/name `deadbeef0001`, the old code always matched the name `deadbeef0001` and returned `deadbeef0002`; the new code returns `deadbeef0001` if that row is first in the dict, so `tokens revoke deadbeef0001` can revoke a different credential than before and leave the intended live token intact. The new `start_pairing` check does not address rows already on disk, so upgrading does not clear the ambiguity.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/auth.py:_find

chunk_findings.detail: The `effect` string says `on, a shell with no token is refused those verbs`, where “those verbs” refers to the operator-only verbs named in `why`. But `tokens pair` is itself an operator-only verb (“Rotation, revocation and pairing are the operator’s”), and the same change’s `docs/guide/tokens.md` says that with `require_operator_token = [REDACTED] `ddflow pair --role operator` still works from a marker-free terminal while no live operator token exists. The upgrade note therefore misdescribes the behavior an operator gets when they turn the knob on: it says every operator-only verb is refused without a token, while the bootstrap `pair` is deliberately not. This is a documentation defect, not a runtime refusal.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/upgrade/unreleased/knob_added.agent.require_operator_token.toml:6

chunk_findings.detail: The `start_pairing` function checks `_taken(data, name)` to ensure a name does not already have a live token or waiting pairing, but it does so *outside* or *concurrently* without verifying whether `name` is validly claimed by an already-stored token that might have expired or been removed, or more critically, `_taken` iterates over all tokens/pairings while `_changing` holds the file lock, but `start_pairing` calls `_person` before checking `_taken`, yet `_person` itself is called without checking the role against `cfg.agent.roles` first, leading to a potential race condition where duplicate active tokens for the same identity can be minted if two pairing requests for the same `name` interleave between `_person` and `_taken` inside the file lock context.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/auth.py:279

chunk_findings.detail: In `_read_code`, if `sys.stdin` is not a tty and `sys.stdin.readline()` is called, it returns `""` when EOF is reached, but `sys.stdin` itself can be `None` in certain non-interactive execution environments (such as some daemon or embedded test contexts), causing `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'isatty'` because the check `sys.stdin is not None and sys.stdin.isatty()` short-circuits the type safety, but the subsequent ternary `sys.stdin.readline() if sys.stdin is not None else ""` checks `sys.stdin is not None`, yet the earlier line `sys.stdin.isatty()` will crash with `AttributeError` when `sys.stdin` is `None` because the outer conjunction evaluates `sys.stdin is not None and sys.stdin.isatty()` where `sys.stdin` is `None` (evaluated as False) EXCEPT if `sys.stdin` is NOT `None` it calls `isatty()`. Wait, if `sys.stdin` is `None`, `sys.stdin is not None` is False, so it short-circuits. But if `sys.stdin` is closed or missing its `isatty` attribute (like a StringIO mocked in tests), calling `sys.stdin.isatty()` raises `AttributeError: 'StringIO' object has no attribute 'isatty'`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/declared/serve.py:32

chunk_findings.detail: `start_pairing` calls `_person(..., first=True)` only after `_changing` has already dropped every store row with `expires <= now`. `_live_operator` then looks only at what remains, so once the last operator token's TTL passes, an agent whose marker is solely a missing proof (`lacks_only_proof`) is treated as the bootstrap caller and may `ddflow pair <name> --role operator` and redeem a new operator token. The same path reopens if that token is revoked. Bootstrap was only meant so a marker-free host could mint the first credential under `require_operator_token`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/auth.py:_person

chunk_findings.detail: `_find` returns the first row whose id or name equals `who`, in insertion order. Token ids are 12 hex chars and names may be the same shape, so given token id `deadbeef0001` named `alice` and a later token named `deadbeef0001`, `revoke`/`rotate` of that name hits `alice` and leaves the named token in place.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/auth.py:_find

chunk_findings.detail: The store row is deleted and the lock released before `log.append(token.revoked)`. `tokens list` is derived from the log. If that append fails (disk full, handler error), a retry cannot find a live row, so it raises and never writes `token.revoked`; the token stays listed active while `verify` rejects it.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/auth.py:revoke

chunk_findings.detail: `lacks_only_proof` treats a call as bootstrap-eligible whenever `_MCP_CALL` is unset, but `is_agent(..., via_mcp=True)` still classifies that same call as "the MCP surface" without requiring the contextvar. Given `_PROOF_REQUIRED` set, no `DDFLOW_AGENT`/`--agent`, `_MCP_CALL` false, and `via_mcp=True`, `is_agent` returns a refusal string while `lacks_only_proof` returns True, so a pairing exemption keyed on `lacks_only_proof` mints an operator token on the MCP surface the refusal path already knows is not a terminal.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/identity.py:lacks_only_proof

chunk_findings.detail: Context setup always calls `ID.clear_credential()` and only rebinds when `DDFLOW_TOKEN` is set or `require_operator_token` is on. A server that follows `with_credential` (the documented non-CLI path) and then builds this context loses the proof for the whole request: `clear_credential` sets the contextvar to None, `bind_env` is skipped, and `with_credential`'s `reset` runs only after the request. Operator role checks and `resolve` therefore see no token even though verification already succeeded.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/context.py:104

chunk_findings.detail: `pair` is declared with the same CLI-only reason as redeem/rotate/revoke (`_REASON`: a minted secret must not enter an agent context) and its payload includes `code`, but the exemption table only adds `path=("tokens",)`. The existing grant/approvals pattern treats that table as what keeps a person's act off the tool surface. An agent-facing dispatch of `pair` therefore returns the one-time code into the tool result and transcript, which is the leak this change says it closed.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/exemptions.py:49

chunk_findings.detail: `other` is only an empty directory, not a second project. `AU.verify(other, Config(), token)` raises `AuthRefused` for a missing store or a non-project path even when project binding is absent, so a token minted for `proj` is treated as cross-project isolation. A verifier that accepts that same token in any other initialized project (shared user store, constant key) still leaves this test green.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_auth_tokens.py:test_a_token_for_one_project_proves_nothing_in_another

chunk_findings.detail: The test only checks `{"token.issued", "token.revoked"} <= PROVENANCE_KINDS`. It never folds a log, compacts, and reads back. If those kinds are listed but compaction still drops `token.issued` / `token.revoked`, the assertion stays true.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_auth_tokens.py:test_the_token_events_survive_compaction

chunk_findings.detail: `_find` now compares every live token’s `name` before checking whether `who` is a token id. `start_pairing` still allows a name that is identical to another token’s id (it only prevents duplicate names, not id/name collisions). Concretely, with live token A id `deadbeef0001` named `alice`, and a later live token B named `deadbeef0001`, `revoke`/`rotate deadbeef0001` now returns token B. If the caller intended to revoke/rotate token A by its id, the wrong token is acted on and token A remains live and unreachable by id while token B exists. Preventing a name from colliding with any live token id, or requiring an explicit `id:`/`name:` disambiguator, would avoid silently targeting the wrong token.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/auth.py:_find

chunk_findings.detail: The new ordering commits the token-store mutation before the audit-log transaction. `_changing` inserts the new token and, for a rotation, pops the old token; the lock is then released. Only afterwards does `log.transaction()` append `token.issued`/`token.revoked`. If that log append raises (for example the log filesystem is full), `redeem` raises so the caller never receives the new secret, but the store is already committed: the old rotated token is dead, the pairing code has been spent by `_spend`, and the new live token row keeps the client name taken until its TTL. Even without a failure, another process running `tokens list` in the gap between `_changing` and `log.transaction()` sees the old token still listed as active while `verify` already rejects it because the store row is gone. This is the same effect-before-record inconsistency as the previously accepted revoke issue, now newly introduced into `redeem`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/auth.py:redeem

chunk_findings.detail: A non-rotation redeem now commits the store (code spent, token hash written) before `log.append`, and any exception there skips `return Minted`. Previously that append sat inside `_changing`, whose non-`AuthRefused` path wrote nothing, so a failed issue did not burn the code. Given a fresh pairing code and `log.append` raising (disk full, handler error), the client never receives `ddft_…`, a retry is refused because the code is gone, and the name stays taken by a hash of a secret that exists only in the failed stack frame. The rotation case is the tradeoff the new docstring describes; the first-issue path has no old token to protect and only regresses the guarantee the removed `_changing` comment stated.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/auth.py:redeem

chunk_findings.detail: The confirmed bootstrap gap is not closed. `start_pairing` still calls `_person(..., first=_operator(cfg, role))`, and the updated docstring and `[agent].require_operator_token` knob still allow a marker-free caller to mint an operator token whenever no live operator row remains. After the last operator token expires or is revoked, an agent whose only marker is a missing proof (`lacks_only_proof`) can `ddflow pair <name> --role operator` and redeem a new operator token. Narrowing `first` to the operator role and documenting the lockout does not stop that call.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/auth.py:_person

chunk_findings.detail: Removing `ID.clear_credential()` leaves a proof installed by an earlier `bind_env` in the same context. Sequence: `DDFLOW_TOKEN` is set, `Ctx` is built and `bind_env` stores an operator `Credential` on the contextvar (and may drop the env var, as the mcp case asserts), then a later request in that same context builds `Ctx` for `status` with no `DDFLOW_TOKEN` and `require_operator_token` false. The new branch does not call `bind_env` and no longer clears, so `ID.credential()` and `ctx.log.agent_id` stay the previous operator. Operator-only checks then succeed for a request that presented no token. The added test only covers `with_credential` nested around one `Ctx` with the default config, so it does not catch this.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/context.py:102

chunk_findings.detail: The new `start_pairing` guard only rejects *new* names shaped like token ids and `STORE_VERSION` is still 1, so rows written by the previous version are not migrated or rejected. A store created before this change can already contain token A with id `deadbeef0001`/name `alice` and token B with id `c0ffee123456`/name `deadbeef0001`, exactly the collision this fix targets. `_find` now returns the first row where `who` matches either `token_id` or `row["name"]`; after upgrading, `revoke deadbeef0001` revokes A if A was inserted first, and revokes B if B was inserted first. In the first case a caller cannot revoke token B by its name, and in the second a caller cannot revoke token A by its id. The previous name/id collision therefore still holds for existing stores.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/auth.py:_find

chunk_findings.detail: The `effect` string states that with `agent.require_operator_token = [REDACTED] “a shell with no token is refused those verbs.” The same change’s `docs/guide/tokens.md` documents the exception: while no live operator token exists, `ddflow pair --role operator` still works from a marker-free terminal, because `pair` is one of the operator-only verbs. So in the no-live-operator-token state a shell with no token is not refused `ddflow pair`; the shipped upgrade note contradicts the behavior the change itself describes for the expiry-recovery path.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/upgrade/unreleased/knob_added.agent.require_operator_token.toml:8

chunk_findings.detail: The new effect sentence says that with `require_operator_token` on, "a shell with no token is refused those verbs, except `ddflow pair --role operator` while no live operator token exists." That exception is stated more broadly than the behavior it describes: the recovery pairing path is only for a **marker-free** shell (`lacks_only_proof`), not for every shell lacking a token. Given `require_operator_token= [REDACTED] no live operator token, and a shell exporting `DDFLOW_AGENT=alice` but no `DDFLOW_TOKEN`, the text implies `ddflow pair --role operator` is allowed, but the agent marker makes `lacks_only_proof` false and the command is refused. The exception should name the marker-free condition; as written it misdocuments the access-control escape hatch.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/upgrade/unreleased/knob_added.agent.require_operator_token.toml:8

chunk_findings.detail: The rewritten `effect` still misstates who the bootstrap exception covers. It says that with the knob on, a shell with no token is refused operator-only verbs except `ddflow pair --role operator` while no live operator token exists. That reads as any token-less shell, including one that still carries an agent marker (`DDFLOW_AGENT`, `--agent`, or the MCP call marker). Bootstrap only opens for a marker-free caller (`lacks_only_proof`) asking for the operator role; the same marker-bearing shell with no token is still refused `pair --role operator` after the last operator token expires or is revoked. The note therefore tells an operator the opposite of that case.
